title: Best Serengeti Camps: Where to Stay by Area, Season and Budget
meta_title: Serengeti Camps: 7 Best Picks by Area, Season and Budget
meta_description: Serengeti camps matched to the migration: where to stay for calving, river crossings and big cats, with cost tiers and park fees. Plan your Tanzania stay.
excerpt: The best Serengeti camps depend on your month: Ndutu for calving, Kogatende for river crossings and Seronera all year. Here is where to stay, what it costs and how many nights to book.
content:
The best Serengeti camps are the ones placed where the wildlife is during your travel month: Ndutu in the south for calving from December to March, the Western Corridor for May to July, Kogatende in the north for Mara River crossings from July to October, and the central Seronera area for reliable big cats all year.

The Serengeti covers about 14,763 square kilometres, so choosing the wrong base can mean four hours of driving a day just to reach the herds. This guide matches Serengeti camps to each area and season, describes well-known properties from their own official information, sets out realistic budget tiers and explains the park fees that sit on top of every room rate.

Quick Facts

  • Park size: about 14,763 km², a UNESCO World Heritage Site in northern Tanzania
  • Main camp areas: central (Seronera), southern (Ndutu), Western Corridor (Grumeti), northern (Kogatende and Lobo) and eastern plains
  • Getting there: about 7 to 7.5 hours by road from Arusha to the central Serengeti, or light-aircraft flights to airstrips across the park
  • Park entry: US$82.60 per non-resident adult per 24 hours in the high season, including VAT (checked October 2026)
  • Extra fee: camps and lodges inside the park add a nightly concession fee, usually built into the room rate
  • Nights needed: three to four nights, ideally split between two areas

Where Are the Best Serengeti Camps Located?

The best Serengeti camps are spread across five zones, and each one shines at a different time of year. Pick the zone for your month first, then the camp. A beautiful camp in the wrong zone is the most common and most expensive mistake on a Tanzania safari.

The Great Migration moves in a rough clockwise loop. The herds spend the short rains and calving season on the southern short-grass plains, move north-west through the centre and the Western Corridor as the long rains end, and reach the far north and the Mara River in the dry season. For the full herd calendar, see our Great Migration month-by-month guide.

AreaBest monthsWhy stay there
Central Serengeti (Seronera)All yearResident lions, leopards and cheetahs, easiest road access, widest choice of lodges
Southern Serengeti and NdutuDecember to MarchCalving season, newborn wildebeest and the predators that follow them
Western Corridor (Grumeti)May to JulyHerds passing through, Grumeti River crossings, large crocodiles
Northern Serengeti (Kogatende, Lobo)July to OctoberMara River crossings with far fewer vehicles than the Kenyan side
Eastern SerengetiNovember to JuneOpen plains, cheetahs and very few other vehicles

Migration timing shifts with the rains every year, so these months are patterns rather than promises. If your dates are fixed, choose a base that gives you a second option within a few hours' drive.

Best Serengeti Camps in the Central Serengeti

Central Serengeti camps suit first-time visitors, shorter trips and anyone travelling outside peak migration months. The Seronera Valley has year-round water, so resident predators stay put, and it is the area most easily reached by road from the Ngorongoro highlands.

The trade-off is traffic. The central area holds the largest number of lodges, so popular sightings can draw several vehicles. Leaving at first light and taking a packed breakfast helps you beat the crowds.

Four Seasons Safari Lodge Serengeti

Four Seasons Safari Lodge Serengeti sits in the central Serengeti and is one of the park's larger luxury properties, with 60 rooms, 12 suites and 5 freestanding villas. Its infinity pool overlooks a watering hole that elephants visit, and there are two active waterholes on the property.

The lodge runs a children's and teens' programme called the Kijana Klub and has a Discovery Centre with wildlife exhibits and a lecture hall. That makes it one of the more practical choices for families who want hotel-style comfort, a pool and activities for children between game drives.

Serengeti Serena Safari Lodge

Serengeti Serena Safari Lodge stands on an acacia-lined ridge and is built as a village of stone, thatched, dome-roofed rondavels arranged around an infinity pool. It has 65 guest rooms and one suite, and its decor uses warm earth tones and Makonde carvings.

This is a classic lodge rather than a tented camp, which suits travellers who prefer solid walls, a larger property and a mid-range to upper mid-range budget. The lodge also offers its own game drives in open-sided six-seat vehicles if you are not travelling with a private guide.

Which Serengeti Camps Are Best for the Calving Season?

For the calving season, the best Serengeti camps are in the south around Ndutu and the southern short-grass plains. From about December to March the herds graze here, and most calves are born over a few weeks, usually from late January into February.

Calving brings intense predator action, because lions, cheetahs and hyenas target the young. Read our Serengeti migration guide for more on the calving months.

Ndutu Safari Lodge

Ndutu Safari Lodge sits beside Lake Ndutu in the south-eastern part of the Serengeti ecosystem. It has 34 simple en-suite cottages built from stone and thatch, with thick walls that keep rooms cool, hot showers and private verandas facing unfenced bush.

The lodge is a long-standing base for watching the migration in the calving season, and it suits travellers who value location over luxury. Note that the Ndutu area lies inside the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, which charges US$70.80 entry per adult per 24 hours plus a nightly concession fee of US$59 for lodge guests (checked October 2026).

Dunia Camp

Dunia Camp is a small tented camp in the south-central Serengeti with seven tents and one family tent. It is run entirely by women and is recommended by its operator for the migration months of roughly March to June and November to December.

Dunia suits families with children aged five and over, solo travellers and anyone who likes an intimate camp with a strong community feel.

Best Serengeti Camps for River Crossings in the North

For Mara River crossings, the best Serengeti camps are in the far north around Kogatende, where the herds gather on the riverbanks from about July to October. The northern Serengeti sees far fewer vehicles than the Masai Mara side, which is why many photographers prefer it.

The north is a long way from Arusha by road, so most guests fly into Kogatende airstrip and combine the north with a night or two in the centre. Our fly-in safari packages show how a flying itinerary saves days of driving.

Sayari Camp

Sayari Camp lies in the Kogatende area, close to the Mara River crossing points. It has 15 suites plus two private Retreats, a contemporary design and an infinity pool, and it suits migration chasers, couples and families who want a high-end stay. The camp closes for the long rains and reopens in June, so check dates if you are travelling in April or May.

Northern Serengeti camps versus the Masai Mara

Camps in the northern Serengeti and the Masai Mara watch the same river, but from different countries. The Mara has more camps and more vehicles at the main crossings; the Serengeti side is quieter but costs more to reach. If you are weighing the two, compare our Masai Mara camps by budget.

Serengeti Camps in the Western Corridor and the East

The Western Corridor and the eastern plains are the Serengeti's specialist areas. The west peaks when the herds pass through in about May to July, while the east suits travellers who want open plains, cheetahs and space without other vehicles.

Kirawira Serena Camp

Kirawira Serena Camp stands on a hilltop in the Western Corridor, within reach of the Grumeti River. It has 25 tents raised on timber platforms, decorated in an Edwardian safari style with four-poster beds. It is a good choice for travellers who want a classic luxury tented camp near the migration's western route.

Namiri Plains

Namiri Plains is in the eastern Serengeti, an area that was closed to visitors for over 20 years to help cheetahs recover and reopened in 2014. The camp has 10 suites, a family suite and two Retreats built with local volcanic stone. It suits photographers and wildlife purists looking for exclusive sightings.

How Much Do Serengeti Camps Cost?

Serengeti camps range from public campsites on the cheapest camping safaris to luxury camps where peak-season rates pass US$1,000 per person per night. Most travellers stay in mid-range lodges and permanent tented camps, usually on full-board terms with meals included.

The estimates below are per person per night, sharing a room, for accommodation only. They are typical published rate bands, not Divulge package prices, and vary with season, area and how many game drives are included.

Budget tierWhere you sleepEstimated cost per person per night
BudgetPublic campsites on a camping safari, or simple lodgesUnder US$200
Mid-rangeLarger lodges and permanent tented campsAbout US$300-700
LuxurySmall high-end camps and premium lodgesAbout US$800-2,000 or more

On top of the room rate you pay park entry of US$82.60 per adult per 24 hours in the high season, set by Tanzania National Parks (TANAPA), plus the nightly concession fee for camps inside the park (checked October 2026). Fees change, so always confirm them before booking. For a full trip budget, read our guide to a Tanzania safari on a budget.

How to save money on Serengeti camps

The simplest saving is timing. April and May bring the long rains and the lowest rates, and some camps close, while November is a shoulder month in many areas. Spending your first and last nights in the Ngorongoro highlands or Karatu, rather than inside the park, also trims costs; see our Ngorongoro Crater lodges guide for those options.

How Many Nights Should You Spend in Serengeti Camps?

Most travellers should spend three to four nights in Serengeti camps, ideally split two and two between two areas. Two nights is the minimum to make the long journey worthwhile, and it leaves only one full day of game viewing.

A split stay gives you two different landscapes and a better chance of finding the herds. Good pairings are Ndutu with the central Serengeti in the calving season, and the central Serengeti with Kogatende from July to October. Our Tanzania northern circuit itinerary shows how the Serengeti fits with Tarangire and the Ngorongoro Crater.

Tented camp, lodge or mobile camp?

Permanent tented camps have proper beds, en-suite bathrooms and canvas walls, so you hear the bush at night. Lodges have solid walls, more rooms and often a pool. Mobile camps move during the year to stay near the migration, which puts you closer to the herds but with simpler facilities such as bucket showers.

Insider Tips

  • Choose the area first: match the zone to your month before comparing camps
  • Book early for July to October: small northern camps fill many months ahead
  • Check opening dates: several camps close during the April and May long rains
  • Ask what is included: confirm whether park and concession fees, drinks and game drives are in the rate
  • Mind the luggage limit: light aircraft usually require soft bags and strict weight limits
  • Pack layers: early morning drives are cool even in the hot months

Packing well matters more in a remote camp, where there are no shops. Our Tanzania safari packing checklist covers clothing colours, layers and camera kit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which area has the best Serengeti camps?

The best area for Serengeti camps depends on your month. Choose Ndutu and the southern plains from December to March for calving, the Western Corridor from May to July, Kogatende in the north from July to October for Mara River crossings, and the central Seronera area at any time of year for reliable lions, leopards and cheetahs.

How much do Serengeti camps cost per night?

Serengeti camps cost roughly under US$200 per person per night at the budget end, about US$300-700 for mid-range lodges and tented camps, and US$800-2,000 or more for luxury camps. These are estimates for accommodation only. Park entry of US$82.60 per adult per 24 hours in the high season and a nightly concession fee come on top (checked October 2026).

How many nights should I stay in the Serengeti?

Three to four nights is the ideal stay in the Serengeti for most travellers. Splitting the nights between two areas, such as Ndutu and the central Serengeti in the calving season, or the centre and Kogatende in the dry season, gives you more variety and a better chance of finding the migration herds.

Are Serengeti camps safe?

Serengeti camps are unfenced, so wild animals can walk through at night, but staff escort guests to and from their tents after dark and give a safety briefing on arrival. Follow the camp rules, stay inside your tent at night and never walk around alone, and a camp stay here is very safe.

Do Serengeti camps close in the rainy season?

Some Serengeti camps close during the long rains, usually in April and May, and several mobile camps move or shut between seasons. Sayari Camp in the north, for example, reopens in June after the long rains. Larger lodges in the central Serengeti generally stay open, so always check opening dates for April and May travel.

Final Thoughts

The best Serengeti camps are the ones in the right place for your month: Ndutu for calving, the Western Corridor from May to July, Kogatende for river crossings and the central Serengeti all year. Split three or four nights between two areas and budget for park fees on top of the room rate.
